newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK economy picks up in Q2, economists urge caution.
newsitem.headline: HK economy picks up in Q2, economists urge caution.

text.p: Hong Kong's economy grew 4.3 percent in the second quarter compared to 3.3 percent in the first quarter and 5.2 percent in the same period last year, Hong Kong's Census and Statistics Department said on Monday.

Economists said the figures confirm signs of economic recovery in Hong Kong, but tempered their optimism by warning that a sharp deceleration in imports might have overstated the improvements in gross domestic product (GDP) growth.

"Yes, the numbers are strong, and the economy will pick up, but not at the rate these numbers suggest. Essentially, the strength in GDP comes from a severe decline in imports," said Arup Raha, senior economist at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong.

Growth in imports sank to 2.2 percent in the second quarter compared to 5.2 percent in the first quarter, caused partly by an inventory adjustment following a build-up last year from the Chek Lap Kok Airport construction project and a fall in private consumption.
Regardless, economists said the figures suggest that a slowdown in Hong Kong's economic growth is bottoming out, albeit at a lower rate than indicated.
"The numbers came out stronger than expected but I am not seeing a very, very strong rebound," said Sun Bae Kim, economist at Goldman Sachs in Hong Kong.

"This does not lead me to revise any figures for the balance of the year," he said. "I see mainly a gradual increase of 4.5 percent for the whole year. That view is basically predicated on a moderate pickup in consumption and some improvement in the external sector."
Private consumption, which makes up 60 percent of GDP, grew only 2.5 percent in the second quarter after rising 3.4 percent in the first quarter.

Economists defended expectations of a consumption-led recovery by pointing to August's five percent increase in retail sales and a second quarter drop in unemployment to 2.8 percent against 3.5 percent in the same period last year.
"Unemployment has been decreasing and we do expect to see a longer-term upwards movement in consumption. A definite trend is underway," said Rob Gvozden, economist at Lehman Brothers.

Among other major GDP components, re-exports grew 6.5 percent in the second quarter against a rise of 7.5 percent in the first quarter, while domestic exports fell 9.0 percent compared to a 7.4 percent decline in the first quarter.
Exports of services grew 5.2 percent compared to the same period last year after rising 9.5 percent in the first quarter.
The Hong Kong government also revised its first quarter GDP figure higher, to 3.3 percent from an original estimate of 3.1 percent.
